Launching the protocol on a chain that does not have one. Changing a chain that already runs it is not done
from this branch — those scripts live on `live`; for a map of the script directories here, see
[`../README.md`](../README.md).

There is no wrapper: **every intent is one forge command**. `--rpc-url <network>` is the only input that
selects a network: it decides where the run connects, and `Chains.detect()` matches that chain id against
`env/<environment>/*.json` to decide which config it reads, so the two cannot disagree. There is no override. The RPC URL
itself and the verification key come from `foundry.toml` (`[rpc_endpoints]`, `[etherscan]`). The signer is always passed explicitly, so a
testnet run and a mainnet run have the same shape and differ only in who signs. The one thing that cannot be
a forge command — bringing up local forks, which needs anvil processes — has a dedicated script here:
`anvil.sh`.

On mainnet the namespace comes from the config, `network.namespace`, like every other thing about the chain.
It is what every mainnet address derives from and it can never be replaced, so it has to outlive any single
key and be the same account on every chain the protocol runs on. Which account that is — a Safe, a Ledger
that delegates to a Safe, a key that delegates to another — is the config's and the gate's business, not this
script's: `LaunchDeployer` supports any of those arrangements without knowing which one it is in.

**The gate comes before the deployment.** Putting the DeployGate on the chain, and naming the namespace's
delegates on it, is not part of a mainnet deployment: another actor does both beforehand, through its own
tooling. Anyone can deploy the gate — `CreateX.deployCreate2(DEPLOY_GATE_SALT, DEPLOY_GATE_BYTECODE)`, both in
`create3-gate/script/DeployGate.d.sol` — and it grants its deployer nothing. A Safe commits only through a gate
already there, so a proposing `commit()` on a chain without one stops before anything is signed.

Each phase **acts as `--sender`**, and how the phase is signed follows from what that account is. Deploying,
it is an executor key. Committing, it is the namespace or a delegate the namespace named through the gate's
`setDelegate`: a key is broadcast from; a Safe cannot sign a forge broadcast, so it is **proposed to** instead,
and the proposal is signed by whoever holds the Ledger, an owner or a proposer of the Safe — the run asks the
device for that account, so nothing names it. `commit()` checks the sender against the gate before anything is
signed; whether the Ledger's account may propose is the Safe transaction service's call, once the proposal is
posted. `deploy()` is an ordinary broadcast from an executor keystore whatever committed: an
executor can only deploy what was already committed, and one transaction per contract is a long sequence to
confirm on a device.

Read off the config rather than an env var on purpose. Root is a constructor argument of nearly everything
wired to it, so the two gate phases have to agree on it exactly — a file both of them read cannot differ
between them the way an environment variable can, and disagreeing costs the whole commitment
("Deployment does not match what was committed"). It is also why the anvil fixtures under `script/anvil/env/`
hold the input half only: a chain config that describes no deployment cannot hand a rehearsal a Root it has no
way to wire.

`cast()` is permissionless because the authority is the ward, not the caller: until Root grants it there is
nothing it can do, and afterwards it does one fixed thing and gives the ward back. Until it has run, the
protocol has no path from Root into the new contracts — no pausing, no recovery, no scheduled upgrades — and
`spoke`, `spokeHandler`, `tokenBridge` and `shareManager` are unendorsed, and so is `vaultRouter` where the vault stack is deployed,
so the vaults do not work and no share token under FullRestrictions can receive a crosschain transfer.

One piece of wiring is not `RootFixes`' either: `Spoke.sender` is left unset, so every `registerAsset`
reverts. A kept Root means a previous release on the chain, whose assets the launch spell
replays into the new Spoke under the ids they already have, and `registerAsset` being permissionless, anyone
could take those ids first. The spell files the `MessageDispatcher` once the replay is done. `RootFixes` must
not, since governance may cast it before the spell is ready, which would reopen the window.

Per-chain quirks — a chain that needs an explicit `--gas-price`, or anything else true of one network and
not the rest — are deployment data, kept beside the configs.

The phases are separate entry points and **always separate forge runs**, on every network — testnets, CI and
anvil included; `run()` refuses to exist precisely so nobody runs both in one. That is how a deployment
separates the two in time — sign the commitment, look at it, come back for the deploy phase later — and it
is the only thing that proves the two agree: the deploy phase rebuilds every init code in a fresh process
and has to land on exactly what the commit phase committed, so anything phase-dependent in a constructor
argument (`msg.sender` is the classic) makes it abort with `NotCommitted` instead of deploying something
else. The addresses are identical either way: the phases are about when things are signed for, never about
where contracts land.

What cannot be done is re-running a phase **from scratch** over a partial deployment. Without `--resume` the
script is simulated again, and it aborts on the first contract whose commitment was already spent
(`Deployment does not match what was committed`). Re-committing does not get around that either: its local walk
redeploys the whole protocol, and those addresses are now taken, so CreateX reverts. So if the broadcast
sequence is gone, the executor's nonce has moved, or the simulation itself is what failed, recovery means
moving the deployment to fresh addresses — a new `env/<environment>-<id>/`, or a version bump.

A committed `(salt, init code)` pair leaves an executor no freedom. The salt fully determines the CREATE3
address and the hash fully determines the code, so an executor can only put the intended code at the
intended addresses, or revert. Authorizing several therefore costs no more trust than authorizing one: none of
them can produce anything the namespace did not commit to. Committing the init code alone would **not** be safe: the executor could then
deploy committed code at an address of its choosing, consume the commitment, and strand the intended address.

Deployment order is enforced outright: a commitment binds each contract to its position, and the gate keeps a
cursor per commitment, so a contract deployed out of turn reverts rather than landing early. The wiring would
catch it a second time — the action batchers wire from their constructors, and a call to a contract that does
not exist yet reverts — but that is a consequence, not the mechanism.

Neither does a superseded commitment linger. Every commit starts a new generation and only the live one can
be deployed from, so a set the namespace replaced cannot be spent afterwards — including the salts the replacement
dropped, which would otherwise stay deployable and let an executor strand a canonical address. Committing
with no salts at all is how a pending commitment is revoked outright, which is what `--sig 'revoke()'` sends,
under the commitment id of the deployment the run's config names: revoking an isolated deployment leaves the
canonical one's commitment deployable, and the reverse.
It reaches the gate on its own rather than walking the deployment, since a commitment worth revoking is
usually one whose addresses are wrong or already half taken, and a walk over a taken address reverts inside
CreateX before it could revoke anything. What was already deployed stays deployed: revoking drops what is
left, it does not roll anything back.

- **delegates** — accounts the namespace lets sign `commit` on its behalf, through
`setDelegate(delegatee, isValid)`. This is how a cold namespace key can be the thing addresses derive from
while another account signs the phase — a warmer key, or a Safe whose owners do. The deployment does not
depend on one, but naming one stays open at any point as an optional step, after which a run commits as
the delegate — broadcast from it when it is a key, proposed to it when it is a Safe. What a
delegate commits waits out the namespace's `setDelay`, and `clear` withdraws every delegation along with
everything they committed. Delegation goes one way and one level deep: `setDelegate` always writes
to the *caller's own* namespace, so a delegate naming one names it in its own, and there is no call that
takes a namespace from the account it is named after. A leaked delegate key can commit, and can be revoked
in one transaction; it can never be walked outwards or used to lock the namespace out.

Two things follow from that shape, and both are deliberate. Revoking a leaked **executor** key means
committing again rather than sending one call — the commitment is replaced whole, executors included, and
committing nothing revokes them along with the salts. Revoking a **delegate** is one call, since delegation
sits beside the commitment rather than in it, and `clear()` is the same call for all of them at once: it
empties the namespace — every delegation, and every commitment made under any id — without needing to know
which ids a leaked key used. Addresses are untouched by it, so what was going to be deployed still can be.
`setDelay(seconds)` bounds a delegation before it is granted: what a delegate commits is not deployable until
that long has passed, which is the window a `clear()` has to land in. What the namespace commits itself never
waits. But the **namespace** itself cannot be replaced: it is what every address derives from, so there is
deliberately no way to move a namespace to another account. That key is what has to be looked after.

- Addresses differ from any deployment made before this contract existed, when the sender was the caller.
Chains already running the protocol cannot be redeployed onto their current addresses.

- Addresses stay equal across chains, and the gate is what enforces it rather than the script. The deployer
is the gate, and CREATE2 scopes the proxy to whoever deploys it, so no address the gate hands out is
reachable from outside it: handing the same salt to CreateX, or to any other deployer, lands somewhere
else. Nothing chain-specific enters the derivation, and the salt is a whole 32 bytes — nothing spent on a
guardian or a redeploy flag — so what separates two namespaces is the full width of a hash. Whatever 32
bytes a script passes, all of that holds.

- Nothing is ever deployed over, and nothing already deployed is reused. This script launches a protocol on a
chain that does not have one; it is not how a release is layered onto a live chain. Rerunning it over an
existing deployment aborts on the first contract whose address is taken, in either phase, and that is
deliberate: the contracts of an earlier release are warded by that release's action batchers, which denied
themselves once they were done, so a later run could not wire them even if it were allowed to redeploy
around them. Shipping a change to a live chain is a dedicated script plus a spell, both on the `live`
branch.

- The standalone scripts there still salt with `msg.sender`, so
their addresses do not derive from the gate and no longer collide with the protocol's. **Their versions must
never overlap with `FullDeployer`'s**: a name and version those scripts share with a gated deployment now
lands on a second, unwired address instead of reverting on a taken one, and the config would record that one
over the address that is actually wired in. Moving them onto the gate as well is the real fix.

- Nobody can put other code at that address. The address is
`keccak256(0xff ‖ CreateX ‖ keccak256(abi.encode(salt)) ‖ keccak256(initCode))[12:]`, so different init code
is a different address; reaching the gate's from any other init code, factory or `CREATE` nonce means
finding a 160-bit preimage. Two things narrow that to something worth checking rather than assuming:
a constructor that reads state can return different runtime code from the same init code, which is why the
gate has no immutables and reads nothing — its own repository pins `DEPLOY_GATE_EXTCODEHASH` against
`type(DeployGate).runtimeCode`, and Solidity refusing that expression for a contract with immutables is what
keeps it true. And the derivation
belongs to the chain: a chain that derives addresses its own way is the one place an address stops speaking
for the code behind it. So every run that touches the gate checks its runtime code against
`DEPLOY_GATE_EXTCODEHASH` before deploying through it, rather than trusting the address.

- `network.namespace` is what needs the continuity instead. Every protocol address derives from it, so it has
to be the same account on every chain, and there is no recovery if it is lost, since nothing can commit in a
namespace on its behalf — a delegate commits *for* it and only while it says so. Whether that account is a
Safe or a key kept cold behind a delegate is a choice the scripts take no side on. Changing the field moves
every address the chain would deploy to, so it is set once, when the config is written.

- `EXECUTORS` names the accounts allowed to run the deploy phase, a comma-separated list read by the commit
phase, which grants them in the namespace: `EXECUTORS=0xabc...,0xdef... forge script ... --sig 'commit()'`. They can
be the namespace's keys or keys with no privilege anywhere else. They are **part** of the commitment, so
changing the set means committing again, and an executor holds no privilege beyond deploying what has been
committed. Required by `commit()` on every network, and at least one — naming nobody would sign a
commitment no key can spend, so it refuses rather than letting it through. `deploy()` never reads it.
- The `DeployGate` holds **no** protocol permissions at any point, so it cannot touch a live deployment.

That is deliberate, and it is the safe direction. These feed indexers, which must not begin *after* a
contract exists; beginning a little before costs some scanning and nothing else. Getting exact per-contract
numbers would mean reading them back from a block explorer afterwards, which is a second command, on a
machine with an API key, for chains whose explorers can answer — and the value of that over "a few blocks
early" did not justify it.
Only an abandoned deployment leaves entries for contracts that never landed, and re-running fixes it.

`env/` stays read-only in `fs_permissions`, so a test or a stray script still cannot rewrite a config through
a cheatcode. The write goes through jq behind ffi, which also keeps the diff down to what actually changed.

`.network.baseRpcUrl` feeds that generator and nothing else — deliberately. Solidity does not parse it, and
no shell script composes a URL from it: everything goes through the alias, so there is one way to reach a
network and one place its API key is named.

A launch deploys the spoke half of the Vault Development Kit (`VaultFactory`, `VaultRequestRouter`,
`VaultRouter`, `SpokeOracle`, the request policies, `ReserveInstantPolicy`, `VaultLiquidityRoute`) only where the network's
config says so:

Set it only on a chain that has activated EIP-7907. `VaultFactory` carries the vault's creation code and both
are over EIP-170, so on any other chain its deployment reverts, and with it the whole `deploy()` run. Nothing in
forge catches that: it size-checks a direct `new`, but not a CREATE made inside a call, and the gate's `deploy`
is one, so both the commit walk and the deploy simulation pass on a chain without EIP-7907 and the run fails on
chain, with the core up and the rest of the commitment stuck behind `vaultFactory`. So `LaunchDeployer` asks the
chain before anything is signed: with the flag set it sends `eth_estimateGas` for a creation as large as the
largest runtime the vault stack deploys, which the node answers under its own code size rule, and refuses the
run when the node does. A creation at exactly the EIP-170 limit is estimated first as the control, so an RPC
that cannot answer reads as that rather than as a chain without EIP-7907. `anvil.sh` runs the refusal against
`local-b` on every PR. Without
the flag nothing of the spoke half is deployed, wired or recorded, and `Env.load()` accepts the config without
those keys (and refuses it with them). The hub half, `OrderBook` and `FeeRequestManager`, is deployed on every
chain whatever the flag says: it fits EIP-170, and a pool's hub settles through it for vaults on any of its
spokes, so a hub chain without EIP-7907 still needs it.

The flag puts no floor under `.network.batchLimit`. No launch deploys a vault, and neither does the hub's
`UpdateVault.DeployAndLink`: a vault is deployed by a transaction on the spoke, `VaultFactory.deploy`, ahead of
the message, which then only registers and links it (src/vaults/ARCHITECTURE.md).

The seeding scripts themselves went with the v1 vaults: `TestData.s.sol` and `BaseTestData.s.sol` drove the
v1 async and sync vault flows, and nothing has replaced them for the Vault Development Kit yet. `script/anvil/anvil.sh`
therefore stops at the deployment. What remains here is the troubleshooting cookbook, which is about a
deployed chain rather than about any one script.

`LayerZeroAdapter` integrates with LayerZero V2 for cross-chain messaging. The adapter uses LayerZero's endpoint V2 with configurable delegate for DVN (Decentralized Verifier Network) and executor settings, as well as send/receive library configuration. Message ordering is not enforced.

`ProtocolGuardian` provides emergency controls and protocol-level management, including pausing, permission scheduling, and cross-chain upgrade coordination. It acts as an intermediary between a multisig safe and the `Root` contract, providing a structured interface for protocol-wide operations. The contract supports instant pause by safe owners (for emergencies) and safe-only unpause to prevent unauthorized resumption.

`OpsGuardian` manages operational aspects of the protocol, specifically adapter initialization, network wiring, and pool creation. It's controlled by an operations-focused multisig safe separate from the protocol guardian's safe, enabling separation of routine operations from critical protocol security decisions. Both are first-time only: it installs a network's first global adapter set, and wires an adapter to a remote chain that adapter is not yet wired to. Replacing a live set or re-pointing a live binding decides which remote contracts the protocol trusts, so each takes a spell: no guardian can do it. Containment is the exception, and deliberately so: `blockSession` remains the ops safe's, because taking a bad set offline must not wait on a timelock.

Gas limits for both legs are configured per pool and share class rather than passed by the caller, so an integrator never has to reason about Centrifuge gas accounting. They arrive from the hub: `fromHub` accepts calls only from the `Envoy`, rejects value, requires the share token to exist, and stores the pair of limits. The remaining wiring is governance-controlled through `file`, which sets the `relayer`, the `spoke`, the `gateway`, and the EVM-to-Centrifuge chain ID mapping.

The `core` module is the protocol's immutable core: the minimal set of contracts required to register pools, account for holdings, manage share classes, and move state between chains. Once deployed, none of it can be upgraded or altered, so builders compose on top of a security surface that does not shift under them.

The local counterpart to `hub`, deployed on every chain a pool operates on. `Spoke` mirrors `Hub`'s role for local operations: asset registration, cross-chain share transfers, request forwarding, and balance-sheet management (share issuance/revocation, asset deposits/withdrawals), with share token deployment and vault registration arriving from the hub through `SpokeHandler`, all backed by `SpokeRegistry`, `Escrow`, and `SnapshotQueue`. The two sides deliberately mirror each other: `Spoke` ↔ `Hub`, `SpokeHandler` ↔ `HubHandler`, `SpokeRegistry` ↔ `HubRegistry`, `SnapshotQueue` ↔ `Holdings`.

`Gateway` batches everything bound for one destination and pool into a single payload and settles cross-chain execution fees onchain as part of dispatch. `MultiAdapter` fans that payload out across one or more configured `adapters` and only forwards it for execution once a configurable quorum of them agrees on the identical payload, so no single adapter can forge a message on its own. See [`messaging/README.md`](./messaging/README.md).
- **Request manager** (`ISpokeRequestManager`) - the spoke-side counterpart to the hub's request manager; the only caller allowed to dispatch outbound requests.

Hooks are optional per-pool contracts that core calls out to at defined points, letting a pool add behaviour without changing core. Core holds only an interface reference and a zero address means the hook is simply skipped, so every hook here is opt-in. Two seams are covered in this module: `ISnapshotHook`, which `Holdings` fires when a network's holdings and issuance become consistent, and `IBridgingHook`, which `HubHandler` consults before a cross-chain share transfer proceeds. Transfer restrictions on the share token itself are a separate seam, documented in [`src/token/hooks`](../token/hooks).

`ShareManager` is a balance sheet manager for hub-driven share issuance and revocation, used for holdings tracked outside the protocol (e.g. investments on chains where the protocol is not live). Every operation is a manager call from the hub arriving through the Envoy, so it matures through the hub policy before execution; no local wallet holds any permission. A single deployment is shared across pools.

- **An escrow** counts as a member and ignores its freeze bit. `freeze` refuses one; `updateMember` accepts one, to no effect. On role checks this means a payout into an escrow passes wherever the equivalent transfer would, which is what a fund of funds needs for a manager claiming an underlying redemption into the top pool's escrow, which holds no membership on the underlying's token. `VaultLiquidityRoute` is not an escrow: it takes the underlying position from the top escrow and is paid by the underlying vault, so under `RedemptionRestrictions`, `FreelyTransferable` and `FullRestrictions` the underlying pool has to make the route a member (`updateMember`). Until it does the route reads no capacity and the top vault falls back to its own cash.

- **A linked vault of the token's own share class** (`isShareClassVault`) cannot be frozen, and a freeze bit set on it before it was linked (its address is predictable) is ignored. The vault holds the shares it revokes between pulling them and the spoke burning them, so freezing it would brick every redemption through it. The exemption is scoped to the token: a vault of another share class, including another pool's, is an ordinary account and can be frozen. On transfers the token is the caller, so the check reads it from `msg.sender`.

A flavor is a `HookPolicies.Policy` saying, for each of five roles, whether the party must be a member, as in the table below. `Refund`, taking back what the account itself put in, has no bit: only a freeze refuses it. The hook is deployed with its encoded mask. A frozen party fails every role, so membership only adds what is asked beyond that. A member is a live membership or an escrow. How an endorsed contract counts is not the flavor's choice: the roles that take or hold shares (`entry`, `transfer`) accept one, since an endorsed contract holds shares mid-flow for the protocol, and the roles that leave the pool (`exit`, `burn`, `payout`) do not, since an endorsed public relay would otherwise let anyone exit through it.

Both entry points reduce to one hand-over, `_canHandOver(token, role, data, from, to)`: the source must not be frozen, and the destination answers to the role. A share movement is classified once (`leg`: a mint, a release out of an escrow, a fulfillment, a burn, or a transfer) and maps to its role, a mint or a release to `entry` and a transfer to `transfer`, while a fulfillment and a burn are decided on the source alone; a role check names its role and both parties. So a flavor cannot allow a hand-over as a role check that it refuses as the equivalent transfer, or the reverse. A transfer brings both parties' hook data, and a role check's is read from the token. Which roles each vault action asks, of whom, is the vault's: `src/vaults/libraries/RoleCheckLib.sol`.
This hook is suitable for pools that want minimal restrictions with the ability to freeze accounts. It uses only the freeze bit of the `hookData` structure, leaving memberlist functionality unused.

This hook suits pools that screen who may subscribe and who may exit, but not who may hold. Because gating the exit is its purpose, the payout receiver must be a strict member (or an escrow), as under `FullRestrictions`, and endorsement does not substitute. Membership is checked again at claim time and not only when the request was submitted, so a `validUntil` that lapses in between can withhold a claim whose assets are already in the escrow or whose shares are already burned. The `max*` views ask with the holder as both parties, so they read zero for an expired holder's claims, except a refund, since `Refund` asks no membership.

`OracleValuation` provides asset valuation via trusted price feeders who can update prices on-chain. Prices are denominated in the pool currency and stored per pool, share class, and asset. The contract uses a quorum of 1 (no price aggregation) and allows pool managers to authorize feeders who can set prices.
1. **ERC-7540 claims are per controller, not per request id.** A claim needs the controller's total claimable, so each controller has a ledger that adds up across positions.

2. **A shared window bucket has an unbounded number of contributors.** Settling must not touch each of them, so the hub callback stays O(1): the settlement is recorded once on the bucket and each contribution is folded into its ledger later.

3. **The hub fills buckets in any order, and in part.** Settlement cannot be walked in sequence: a bucket the manager has not touched must not block newer ones that settled. So there is no cursor, each position stands alone, and a claim looks at the latest few positions, not the oldest.

4. **A controller can hold any number of positions.** It opens them itself, its operators open them for it, a sponsor the pool allowed can fund them, and on a vault without an instant lane anyone can fund or transfer one to it. No cost or limit may depend on how many it holds.
5. **Views must be cheap and match what a claim would do.** They read the horizon's settled slices and per-controller pending totals, never every position.

In an instant deposit of `gross` assets, the caller pays the fee to the recipient and the rest to the escrow, or the whole `gross` to the escrow when the fee is retained; either way the shares minted are worth `gross - fee`. In an instant redeem, shares worth `gross` are burned and the receiver gets `gross - fee`; the escrow pays the fee out to the recipient, or keeps it. `mint` and `withdraw` are the exact-out forms: the policy grosses the net up, rounding up. A negative fee is a rebate paid by the recipient, which must then be set; no shipped policy answers one. A pool that wants both a manager fee and a holder spread names a splitter contract as the recipient. The splitter is a balance sheet manager: a permissionless `split()` pays the manager's share and deposits the rest back into the escrow, where it is retained. It runs after the trade, not inside it: until it is called the holders' share sits in the splitter and NAV is understated, and the splitter's manager role is not scoped to this job, so it should be minimal and immutable.
| `requestRedeem` | `Exit` of the owner, and of a distinct controller from the owner |

- **Gone:** the investor-initiated cancellations (`cancelDepositRequest`, `cancelRedeemRequest` and their claims; cancellation is the manager's, at order level, and the cancelled amount is claimed on the opposite side), `authorizeOperator` and its typehash, `isPermissioned` (ERC-7714), `setEndorsedOperator`, `priceLastUpdated`, `deploymentChainId`, `hasPermissions`, the router's `enable` and `disable` and its `cancel*` calls.

- **Deployment:** the vault is over EIP-170, so it deploys only on chains with EIP-7907, and the share token's hook has to implement `IRoleHook` (the four shipped hooks do), so a live share token needs its hook swapped. There is no migration of open v1 requests in this PR.
| `ISettlementObserver` (optional) | reactions to each settlement, told once with its fill or cancellation (true-ups, accrual, registers) | none shipped |

The kit provides the rest: the vault's state and both flows, pro-rata bucket settlement with partial fills and a per-controller claimable ledger, request ids and transport, the segregated escrow with reservations and double-entry books behind NAV (from `src/core`), cross-chain messaging, batching and issuance, and conformance with ERC-4626, ERC-7540, ERC-7575, ERC-8161 and ERC-165, apart from the deviations the specification lists (previews and `max*` on a dual-mode vault, no allowance flow on instant exits, no self-operator). There is no upgrade path and no setter: configuration is constructor-fixed, and a change ships as a new vault (a new `variant` runs it beside the old one).

- **Blocking is reverting.** A request, instant or settlement hook that reverts stops that action, which is how allowlists, gates and lockups are written. Hooks that must not block (accrual, registers) guard their own external calls.

- **A bad plugin of a vault breaks that vault only.** The vault's five plugins are fixed at construction and scoped to it, so a faulty one cannot affect another vault of the pool or the protocol; [Trust in pool-chosen components](SPECIFICATION.md#trust-in-pool-chosen-components) lists what a pool can and cannot do to its investors.

* **FV**: where the property is formally verified. `-` everywhere today: there are no Certora specs
for `src/vaults` yet, so this column doubles as the work list for a first FV pass.

The ERC-7540/ERC-4626 conformance rows were cross-checked against the property set from the Cyfrin /
alexzoid formal-verification report on Accountable Credit Vaults (October 2025), which verifies an
async-redeem vault against 16 EIP-7540 and 40 EIP-4626 rules. Where that vault is stricter than this
one the difference is deliberate and recorded: it enforces an owner-or-operator check on
`requestRedeem` (ERC-7540 mandates supporting the ERC-20-approval flow instead), and it is fully
async so its previews always revert, which a dual-mode vault cannot do.

A controller is in **async mode** on a side when they have anything claimable or a request pending on that side, and in
**sync mode** (instant) on it otherwise, so a pending deposit leaves the instant redeem lane open; the 2-argument ERC-4626
entrypoints route on that distinction. On a vault with an instant lane only the controller, its operator or a **sponsor**
(a payer the vault's instant policy accepts, from a per-vault list the pool sets) can credit a controller a request or a
transferred position. A sponsor funds a position without any say over its claims. On a vault without an instant lane
anyone can credit any controller, and a transfer is a plain ERC-8161 push. A cancellation
carries two amounts: **gross** retires the pending request and releases its reservation, **net** is
what the investor may claim; the difference is a retained fee.

Every contract in this stack outside the vaults themselves is a **per-network singleton shared by all
pools**: `VaultFactory`, `VaultRequestRouter`, `SpokeOracle`, the request policies (one instance per
configuration), `ReserveInstantPolicy`, `VaultLiquidityRoute`, and hub-side `OrderBook` and
`FeeRequestManager`. `BasinLiquidityRoute` is one per venue, shared by every pool that draws on it. A vault is per position; the
things it points at are not. That is a deliberate choice, and it makes "which pool is this call for"
a security boundary rather than a bookkeeping detail, because several of these hold manager rights on
every pool that uses them.

* **State is keyed by pool or by vault.** Orders are `[poolId][scId][assetId][requestId]`, fees
`[poolId][assetId]`, observers `[poolId]`, policy state `[vault]`. Nothing is keyed by a share class
or a local id alone, so one pool's writes cannot land in another's slot.

* **Callers are checked against the pool they claim.** The Spoke gates every balance-sheet call on the
caller being a manager of that pool, `spoke.request` on being that pool's registered request
manager, and the policies on `vault == msg.sender`.

* **Identity comes from the registry, never from a caller-supplied address.** `vaultDetails` is the
sole authority on which pool a vault belongs to. A contract asked `poolId()` directly can answer one
way while a configuration call is validated and another once it is acted on, which is exactly how a
manager of one pool would reach another (`CrossPoolIsolation`).

The request and instant policies, the liquidity route, the oracle, the settlement observer, the share
token's hook and the OrderBook's request observer are the pool's choice, and the stack calls them
plainly: no gas caps, no fallback values, no ceilings applied over their answers. The exceptions guard a
view or a conversion rather than an answer: a capacity is clamped to what converts, a rebate to zero in a
quote, and each underlying's quote in `VaultLiquidityRoute` to `QUOTE_GAS`, the one place the stack caps gas. A component that
reverts, burns gas or misreports harms that pool's own users, not other pools or the protocol. Where
an actor the pool did not choose can reach a path (another pool's vault behind `VaultLiquidityRoute`,
a third-party venue behind `BasinLiquidityRoute`, an investor, a keeper), the
stack catches ordinary reverts instead of capping gas. Gas a component needs is priced in `GasService`
or funded by the pool through extra gas, never capped in a contract apart from that one quote.

Three `n` properties in the tables below are `n` not because the code is wrong but because the safe configuration cannot
be enforced from inside a vault whose features depend on the permissive one. A pool is expected to
satisfy all three.

1. **A restricted share class is gated by its own hook.** `requestRedeem` must support the ERC-20-approval
flow, and the share leg it uses is an authorized transfer, which reaches the hook's `onERC20AuthTransfer`
but which the shipped hooks do not restrict. The vault therefore asks the share token's current hook the role checks of every vault action, so
the gate cannot be left off a vault, and a hook without the `IRoleHook` surface fails closed. That authorized
transfer is the share token's registrar `authTransferFrom`, which `IRegistrar` makes an optional capability
with no way to ask for it. The vault also burns shares through it (the redeem settlement, a redeem
cancellation and the instant exits), so a share class whose registrar lacks it cannot serve async or
instant redemptions, and its `requestRedeem` and `revokeShares` revert. Deposits are unaffected. Check the
registrar before linking a vault to a share class.

3. **A shared liquidity route is shared across pools.** The venue's liquidity is not reserved per
vault, so every vault enabled on one liquidity route draws on the same venue, including vaults of
other pools. A pool cannot be starved into insolvency by this (a draw that cannot be met reverts,
and the payout is bounded by the escrow reservation either way) but its instant-exit capacity is
only as reliable as the behavior of every other pool enabled on the same route. Per the
deployment model above a route is a singleton, so the answer is not a second instance but a
credit line per vault: `BasinLiquidityRoute` bounds each vault's outstanding receivable by the
lower of a limit its pool sets through the Envoy and a credit the venue's liquidity provider sets
directly, so the venue consents to every pool that draws on it and bounds what each may owe. What
it does not do is partition the venue: lines that together exceed the venue's liquidity are each
quoted against the whole of it, and whoever draws first takes it. `VaultLiquidityRoute` has no such
line: its venue is each underlying vault's instant lane, which sees the route as one caller for
every pool, so the underlying's own pool consents to each routing vault by name instead (see the vault liquidity route section).

**Gas benchmarks assume the cancun schedule.** `GasService`'s benchmarks are taken with the bytecode the
chains run, compiled for cancun, executed under cancun, while every chain that can take vaults runs a later
fork (EIP-7907 at least). Prague executes the vault paths at the same price: the `EndToEnd` benchmark run with
`FOUNDRY_EVM_VERSION=prague` reproduces the cancun `requestCallback` measurement exactly. Osaka reprices nothing these
paths execute (its changes are MODEXP, a new `CLZ` opcode and the EIP-7825 transaction cap), and the pinned
toolchain cannot execute it or anything later, since solc 0.8.28 tops out at prague. What a later fork can
move is EIP-7907's own per-word charge for cold-loading code past 24,576 bytes (~0.7k for the vault, ~1k for
the factory on each cold call). It is not in the benchmarks and no reserve is added for it, a deliberate gap
at about 0.1% of a callback. The vault's deployment is not a message: it is a spoke transaction ahead of
`DeployAndLink` (see `VaultFactory`), paid by whoever sends it, so no benchmark depends on code deposit. A
message that runs short fails on the spoke and is retried with more gas rather than lost.

| Only the vault itself can draw liquidity, and only within its credit line | y | - | BasinLiquidityRoute | `msg.sender == vault`, and the receivable after the draw may not exceed `min(limit, credit)`: the pool's limit, set through the Envoy and bound to the vault's own pool, and the venue's credit, set by the basin's liquidity provider. Either side setting zero disables the vault |

| Provided liquidity is paid to the drawing vault, which forwards it to the escrow | y | - | BasinLiquidityRoute, LiquidityRouteIntegration | The vault measures its own balance across `provide`, a balance only it moves while it holds its lock, forwards everything that arrived to the escrow and notes the drawn amount with `noteDeposit`, so an under-delivering route is never paid out of other funds in the escrow (`InsufficientLiquidity`). Measured at the escrow instead, a route reentering a sibling vault of the pool could pass that vault's deposit off as delivery |

| A route needs no protocol authority | y | - | FundOfFundsBasin, BasinLiability | Root is the only ward of each route, there to recover tokens sent to it (`Recoverable`); no route holds other protocol authority, and `BasinLiquidityRoute` is deployed by hand per venue. `BasinLiquidityRoute` books each draw in the pool's escrow, so it must be a spoke manager of each pool that draws on it, a minter of that pool's `AccountingToken` ids, and pass that pool's spoke policy for depositing and withdrawing the liability token; without them it reports no capacity. `VaultLiquidityRoute` releases the pool's own holdings through `spoke.withdraw` and `noteDeposit`, so it must be a spoke manager of each pool that uses it and pass that pool's spoke policy; without either, instant exits through it revert |
| The receivable can never go negative or be over-repaid | y | - | BasinLiquidityRoute | Checked arithmetic on the decrement |
| `available` never reverts on the venue's state | y | - | BasinLiquidityRoute | A venue whose quote reverts or answers short reads as no liquidity |

| A pool where the draw cannot be booked has no Basin capacity | y | - | BasinLiquidityRoute, BasinLiability | `available` is zero unless the route is a spoke manager of the vault's pool, a minter of its accounting tokens, and the liability token a registered spoke asset, so the vault's `max*` never advertise a draw that reverts. A draw without them reverts in the booking (`NotManager`, `NotMinter`, `UnknownAsset`), so a pool cannot draw unbooked. The pool's spoke policy cannot be asked in a view |

| `available` is a per-vault entitlement | n | - | BasinLiquidityRoute | The line is a bound, not a reservation: vaults whose lines together exceed the venue each see the venue's liquidity, and they need not belong to the same pool, so one pool's instant exits can consume liquidity another pool was counting on. Advisory by contract, so overstating it only makes the redemption revert, but see Deployment constraints |

| Repayment is permissioned | y | - | BasinLiquidityRoute | Only a spoke manager of the vault's own pool (`spokeRegistry.manager`) may repay, since repaying reopens the vault's line. Repaying also withdraws the booked liability as far as the route still can: a route without its manager or minter role, or an escrow whose liability balance another manager moved, still takes the repayment and reduces the receivable, leaving the rest booked (`BasinLiabilityLeftBooked`) for the pool to clear with its own roles. The payer is `msg.sender`, and the destination is fetched live from the venue on every call, so the venue can redirect where repayments go |

| `forward` is optional | y | - | VaultLiquidityRoute, BasinLiquidityRoute | A route pulls what it wants and returns; a route that forwards nothing is a valid no-op that leaves the assets idle, and an un-forwarded amount is not an error. Both shipped routes are redeem-side only and no-op it |

| A liquidity route cannot stall settlement or the instant deposit lane through `forward` | n | - | LiquidityRouteIntegration | Deliberate: `forward` runs inside `approveDeposits`, a hub callback, and inside instant issuance, and is called plainly (trust in pool-chosen components), so a reverting route fails the callback, which the gateway keeps for retry, and the instant deposit. Its gas is not in `GasService.requestCallback`: a pool with a forwarding route funds it through the fulfillment's `extraGasLimit`. `provide` is plain too, since an instant redemption it cannot fund must revert |
| The cost of provided liquidity is priced by the route | n | - | - | Deliberate: priced as an exit fee by a composed instant policy, so the route stays a pure liquidity provider |

| A localId cannot overflow into the vault field | y | - | VaultRequestIdLib | `localId` is typed `uint96` at every producer and validated by the ABI decoder, so a wider value cannot be smuggled in. A policy's own counter arithmetic is its own obligation |

| An unrecognized message type is rejected | y | - | RequestMessageLib, RequestCallbackMessageLib | But not through the custom error: a type byte above the enum maximum panics on the enum cast, and the `Unknown*Type` errors are reachable only for a type/variant mismatch or the zero variant |

| A truncated payload is rejected | y | - | RequestCallbackMessageLib | The byte-slicing helpers bounds-check and revert `SliceOutOfBounds`, so a payload shorter than its type requires cannot be misread |

* **Medusa.** `timeout` 3600 s (bounded; `--timeout` overrides), `stopOnFailedTest` false so one failure does not hide
the rest, and `failOnArithmeticUnderflow`, `failOnDivideByZero`, `failOnOutOfBoundsArrayAccess` on: handlers swallow
reverts with try/catch, so a panic that reaches the top frame comes from harness code (ghosts, clamps) and is a
harness bug. Medusa is not in CI and has not been run against this suite here (not installed); `medusa.json` was
checked against the documented keys only. Echidna's 300 ETH contract balance is mirrored in
`targetContractsBalances`.

* **Slither.** Off (`disableSlither`): slither-analyzer 0.11.5 and 0.10.4 both crash on this repo, and Echidna then
continues without it anyway. The cost (constants and function information for the generator) has not been measured.

* Hub and spoke share a chain, so messages apply synchronously; cross-chain delivery is the messaging
suite's.

* Full-exit liveness (`vault_claimMax`) is asserted only while the escrow is not over-reserved: a manager
may reserve ahead of arrival, and `withdrawReserved` pays a claim only out of the unreserved balance.
* The share-token recipient set excludes endorsed contracts, which the hook admits as recipients by design.

* `property_availableGtQueued` is not ported: it is a known break (out-of-band `noteDeposit` can queue
increases not backed by held tokens), recorded as `n` in the specification.

* Pool P's price manager and NAV manager calls are sent as those contracts, not produced by a NAV report: pool N
covers the report path, without a policy.

* A vault whose manager role the pool withdrew (`hub_setVaultManager`) is assumed not to happen in production.
Its async `maxMint` and `maxWithdraw` still offer the full claim, since the views read only the share hook, while
the claim reverts in `Spoke`; the suite only bounds those views for such a vault, and the claim handlers skip it.

* A holding worth more than `type(uint128).max` of the asset is assumed not to happen in production:
`previewRedeem` and `convertToAssets` revert on it. Only the fuzzed extreme prices reach it, and
`property_maxViewsAreExecutable` accepts the refusal only when `convertToAssets` overflows too.

Consequence for coverage reports: `src/core/messaging/{Gateway,MultiAdapter}.sol` **must** show substantial line coverage after a real campaign. As of the current tip a 3M-call Echidna run gives `MultiAdapter` 147/149 and `Gateway` 158/162, with the batching path also covering every logic line of `TransientArrayLib`, `TransientStorageLib` and, through the long-message batches, `TransientBytesLib`. Every `Gateway` and `MultiAdapter` LOGIC line is covered: the remaining 4 and 2 are state/immutable declarations, which Echidna does not attribute. Coverage of `src/` saturates early: a 3M local run and a 100M Recon Cloud run produced byte-identical per-file numbers, so a shortfall there is a missing handler, not a short campaign. The harness's own cross-session branches are slower: a fresh-corpus 3M run missed `gateway_retry`'s baseline bump for a failure funded before the session, which the accumulated corpus reaches. That is why the corpus is kept across handler additions (see Config and corpus). A report showing 0 for either is an attribution bug in the build, not an accurate measurement. See [Coverage attribution](#coverage-attribution) below.

- `blockSession`/`unblockSession`, the `vote`/`execute` split, `Gateway.clearFailedMessage`, and the `CannotBeReceivedLocally`/`SourceMismatch` guards are all in scope. `Gateway.blockOutgoing` and `recoveryIndex` no longer exist.

| `targets/StandbyTargets.sol` | The StandbyAdapter's own surface. `standby_forward` (asserts SB2: one credit consumed, the same bytes relayed once through the underlying with gas `(gasLimit + receiveCost) * 64/63`, the caller refunded). Negatives SB3 (forward without a credit → `NotForwardable`), SB3b (a credited payload under another gas limit → `NotForwardable`), SB4 (forward below the underlying's quote → `NotEnoughValue`), SB5 (`send` from anyone but the MultiAdapter → `NotEntrypoint`), SB6 (`handle`/`vote`/`execute` from anyone but the underlying → `NotUnderlying`). Credits come from the gateway targets' dispatches while the standby is in a set; its inbound votes go through `_inbound`. Inherits `GatewayTargets`. |
| `mocks/MockProtocolPauser.sol` | Trivial. `setPaused` is intentionally unauthenticated. |

- **Wrapped hash** `keccak256(2-byte sessionId ++ payload)`. What `SimpleAdapter.send` records as `lastSentPayloadHash`. Used ONLY by the outbound S1/S2 assertions in `GatewayTargets.sol` and the two Foundry send tests. It is not a vote key; do not "fix" these to `_voteKey`.

Reading the wrong vote key fails SILENTLY. `votes()` returns an all-zero array for an unknown key, so M4 reports `positiveSum == 0 <= deliveries` and passes vacuously, and V2's, Alex-1's and G5's clean-slate preconditions stop constraining anything. `test_voteKey_addresses_the_live_tally` is the guard: it asserts the vote key sees a live tally AND that the bare wrapped hash does not. Keep it.

These are NEVER reset by reconfigure. They validate that protocol behaviour stays correct across session transitions, which is the original motivation for the suite: an adapter-set reconfiguration must not let a stale, already-counted delivery execute a second time.
The pre-deliver `_captureBaselines` + post-success `_recordSuccessfulDelivery` split ensures reverts pollute neither domain.

This PASSES under the multi-session design, because votes are keyed by a session-bearing key, so a stale replay counts under the OLD session's threshold of ≥ 2 and cannot re-execute. The target replays the original wrapped bytes (stale sessionId prefix) and asserts callCount is unchanged; it stays live as a regression guard. Preconditions are a clean vote slate for the wrapped payload and threshold ≥ 2, since threshold-1 duplicate re-execution is by-design parallel-message semantics rather than the replay bug. The complementary kill-switch is `blockSession` on the old session, which rejects stale replays outright and is asserted inline in `multiAdapter_blockSession`.
5. **Sentinel `t(true, ...)` properties are forbidden.** Live enforcement goes in negative target functions. Document the property in NatSpec near the target, not as a no-op property.

6. **The test contract (`address(this)`) is the deployer and ward** of both `Gateway` and `MultiAdapter`. `mocks/BatcherActor.sol` is additionally a `Gateway` ward, because `send` is `auth` and it must call it from inside the `withBatch` callback; that is additive, not a move to a per-actor pattern. Don't replace this with a per-actor pattern without re-thinking auth on the `onlyAuthOrManager` surfaces (`setAdapters`, `blockSession`/`unblockSession`, `gateway.handle`, `clearFailedMessage`) and on the `updateManager` / manager-submission paths `ManagerActor` exercises.

8. **State-mutating targets with inline asserts** (`multiAdapter_blockSession`, `multiAdapter_unblockSession`, `multiAdapter_reconfigure`, Alex-1) must NOT end with `require(false)`. Their state change is the point.

9. **Adapter activeness is always read LIVE** via `_activeList(pool)`/`_isActive(pool, adapter)` in `Setup.sol`, never mirrored in a ghost. The Alex-1 target installs non-prefix sets such as `[adapter1]`, and a "first N of adapter0..2" count ghost misrepresents them. That produced false positives in `oldAdapter_mustRevert` and V2.

`echidna-messaging.yaml` deliberately omits `testLimit`, `workers`, `seqLen`, `timeout`, `symExec` and `seed`, so it works on Recon Cloud (where the UI governs run params) and locally (where CLI flags do). Do NOT add a `timeout`, since it would cap a long cloud campaign early.

Cloud jobs currently build with the default foundry profile, so treat `src/**` coverage from a cloud report as unusable until that is resolved. Property results are unaffected, since only the source mapping breaks.

- **Outbound batching and underpaid batches are now covered**, so `property_G1_isBatching_false` is no longer a tautology: `isBatching` genuinely goes true within a transaction. What remains are BRANCH gaps whose lines all execute, so line coverage will not show them:

- **`NotPayable`** (a send carrying value inside a batch) and a non-zero `withBatch` `callbackValue` both need the tester to hold ETH. `echidna-messaging.yaml` deliberately sets no `balanceAddr`/`balanceContract`, unlike `echidna.yaml`, so fuel is always 0. Adding a balance would change `msg.value` semantics for every payable handler and risks local/cloud divergence, so it is a deliberate deferral rather than an oversight.

- **`BatchTooExpensive`** cannot trip: `MockMessageGas.messageOverallGasLimit` returns 0, so the accumulated batch gas limit never approaches `MAX_BATCH_GAS`. The guard executes, the branch is unreachable.
- **`ReentrantBatchCreation`** needs `withBatch` (or `send`) re-entered from inside an adapter's `send` during the dispatch loop, i.e. an adapter mock that calls back into the gateway.
- Note that the end-to-end suite uses a `MockGateway`, so this suite's number is the protocol's total stateful `Gateway` coverage.

- **Multi-remote.** Only `REMOTE_CENTRIFUGE_ID=2` has adapter sets, so per-cId accounting (two remotes sharing payload hashes, `callCount` and `failedMessages` per cId) is out of reach, and so is a batch spanning two remotes. Multi-pool is covered (see [Pools](#pools)); closing this needs a second remote id with its own adapters and the ghosts' `REMOTE_CENTRIFUGE_ID` reads generalised the way the pool reads were.

- **`AdapterFailover.UnexpectedValue`** (`fromHub` with value) needs the envoy to hold ETH, the same deferral as `NotPayable` above. An unknown `HubCall` kind panics in the enum decode and is not fuzzed.

- **`SimpleAdapter` doesn't model Axelar's pull-based commandId queue.** The Alex-1 target works around this by orchestrating the reconfigure inside the target. A higher-fidelity adapter mock with a `pendingDelivery(hash)` queue surviving reconfigure would let more attack patterns emerge organically.

- **Session-id exhaustion** (`activeSessionId == type(uint16).max`), where `setAdapters` panics `0x11` instead of wrapping and permanently bricks reconfiguration for that (cId, pool). Unreachable in fuzz sequences since `seqLen` 50 is far below 65535, and not modelled here. The DoS shape is a protocol-design question rather than a harness gap.
